Medibuddy Insurance Analysis

Power BI step-by-step guide, insights for the 8 questions, and ML model results (1,338 policies, data merged 1:1 on Policy no., no missing values or duplicates).

Key takeaway: smoking status is the dominant cost driver (smokers = 20% of policies, 49% of spend), amplified by obesity. Age is a steady secondary driver. Gender, region and dependents are weak or indirect. Price on smoker × BMI × age band rather than gender or region.

Note on visuals: I can’t run Power BI here, so the charts below are matplotlib renderings built from your actual data to show what each Power BI visual will look like. Colors and layout are close to Power BI defaults; fonts and tooltips will differ.

Part A – Power BI step-by-step

  1. Get data: Home → Get data → Excel workbook. Load Medibuddy_insurance_data_personal_details (Sheet1) and Medibuddy_Insurance_Data_Price. Choose Transform Data.
  2. Power Query: Use first row as headers on both. Rename charges in INR → Charges. Check types (age, children, bmi, Charges numeric; others text). Trim the odd trailing space in the second sheet name if present.
  3. Combine (Workflow step): Home → Merge Queries as New → select Policy no. in both → Inner join → expand all columns except the duplicate key. Name the result Insurance. Do not use Append: that stacks rows, it does not join columns.
  4. Close & Apply, then add the columns/measures below (Modeling → New column / New measure).
BMI Category =
SWITCH(TRUE(), Insurance[bmi]<18.5,"1-Underweight", Insurance[bmi]<25,"2-Normal", Insurance[bmi]<30,"3-Overweight","4-Obese")

Age Band =
SWITCH(TRUE(), Insurance[age]<=25,"18-25", Insurance[age]<=35,"26-35", Insurance[age]<=45,"36-45", Insurance[age]<=55,"46-55","56-64")

Total Policies = COUNTROWS(Insurance)
Avg Charges    = AVERAGE(Insurance[Charges])
Median Charges = MEDIAN(Insurance[Charges])
Total Charges  = SUM(Insurance[Charges])
Smoker % = DIVIDE(CALCULATE([Total Policies], Insurance[smoker]="yes"), [Total Policies])
Smoker Spend Share = DIVIDE(CALCULATE([Total Charges], Insurance[smoker]="yes"), [Total Charges])
Discount Cost 5% =
CALCULATE([Total Charges], Insurance[smoker]="no", Insurance[BMI Category]="2-Normal") * 0.05

5. Build pages (one per question) with the visuals listed under each insight below; add slicers for Sex, Region, Smoker, Children; use Format → Edit interactions so slicers cross-filter. 6. Finish with the dashboard page:

Part B – Insights and the matching Power BI visuals

1. Does gender matter?

Marginally on average, not in practice. Males average ₹13,957 vs ₹12,570 for females (Welch p=0.036), but medians are almost identical (₹9,370 vs ₹9,413; Mann-Whitney p=0.73). The gap comes from more male smokers (23.5% vs 17.4%). Within smokers/non-smokers, gender barely changes cost. Do not use gender as an underwriting constraint (also legally risky); smoking explains it.

Power BI build: Clustered column: Sex × Average of charges; Clustered column: Sex × Median; 100% stacked column: Sex / Smoker count. Extra: Slicer: Sex.

2. Average spend per policy

Mean ₹13,270, median ₹9,382 (right-skewed, skew 1.5). Non-smokers ₹8,434 vs smokers ₹32,050, i.e. 3.8×. Smokers are 20% of policies but 49% of total spend. Use the median or segment-level averages for pricing, as the mean is pulled up by large claims.

Power BI build: Card: Average of charges; Card: Median; Histogram (bins on charges); Column chart: smoker × average. Extra: Cards.

3. Separate policies by region?

Statistically significant (ANOVA p=0.031) but weak. Southeast averages ₹14,735 vs ₹12,347 in the southwest. The cause is mix: southeast has the most smokers (25%) and highest BMI (33.4). Within smokers/non-smokers the regional spread is small. Recommendation: no separate regional products; at most a modest loading in the southeast, or better, price on smoking and BMI.

Power BI build: Column: Region × Avg charges; Clustered column: Region × Smoker; Map (filled) by region if geocoded. Extra: Slicer: Region.

4. Do dependents matter?

Weakly (correlation 0.07; ANOVA p=0.006). 0–1 children ≈ ₹12.4–12.7k, 2–3 children ≈ ₹15.1–15.4k; 4–5 children show lower averages on tiny samples (25 and 18 policies, so unreliable). Not a strong pricing driver. At most a light family-size tier.

Power BI build: Column: Children × Avg charges; Line: Children × Smoker. Extra: Slicer: Children.

5. Does BMI help predict claims?

Yes, but only through smokers. Obese (BMI≥30) average ₹15,552 vs ₹10,409 normal. Among smokers BMI correlates 0.81 with charges (obese smokers ₹41,558 vs ₹19,942 normal-BMI smokers); among non-smokers just 0.08 (₹8,843 vs ₹7,686). The cost cliff is obese + smoker.

Power BI build: Column: BMI category × Avg charges; Scatter: bmi × charges, legend = smoker; Clustered column BMI category × Smoker. Extra: Calculated column: BMI Category.

6. Smoker vs non-smoker?

Yes, the single most important factor. Smokers cost ₹32,050 vs ₹8,434 (p<0.001), explain ~most of the model's importance (smoker and smoker×BMI terms together), and every age band and region shows the same gap. Collect smoking status (with verification such as cotinine tests or declarations with penalties) and price a smoker premium.

Power BI build: Box plot (custom visual) or column; Pie/donut: Sum of charges by smoker. Extra: Slicer: Smoker.

7. Does age create a barrier?

Cost rises steadily with age: ₹9,087 (18–25) to ₹18,796 (56–64), r=0.30. Smokers cost ₹28k–40k at every age, non-smokers climb ₹4k to ₹14k. So age is a graded loading, not a cut-off. Age bands with a smoker flag are the right rating structure; refusing older applicants is not justified by the data.

Power BI build: Column: Age band × Avg; Line: Age band × Smoker; Scatter: age × charges. Extra: Calculated column: Age Band.

8. Discounts based on BMI?

Only for non-smokers. Non-smoker average rises from ₹5,533 (underweight) → ₹7,686 (normal) → ₹8,258 → ₹8,843 (obese), so a wellness discount is supportable at modest size. Smokers show no discount case, since even normal-BMI smokers cost ₹19,942. Simulation: a 5% discount on normal-BMI non-smokers costs ₹67k (0.4% of total spend); 10% costs ₹134k (0.8%). Suggested: 5–10% for non-smokers with BMI 18.5–25, tied to annual re-check; loading for smoker + BMI≥30.

Power BI build: Column: BMI category × Avg charges, filtered Smoker = no; Card: discount cost via DAX. Extra: Page filter: Smoker = no.

Part C – Machine-learning model

Approach: 80/20 split (stratified on smoker), 5-fold CV on training data only, engineered features (smoker×BMI, obesity flag, smoker×obese, age²), then RandomizedSearchCV on Gradient Boosting and Random Forest.

ModelCV R²Test R²MAE (₹)RMSE (₹)
Linear (engineered)0.8760.8412,5835,017
Poly-2 Ridge0.8730.8382,6195,057
Random Forest default0.8460.8063,0155,531
Gradient Boosting default0.8640.8282,7395,208
Random Forest tuned0.8710.8372,6915,078
Gradient Boosting tuned0.8700.8362,7485,092
Honest read: every reasonable model plateaus at test R² ≈ 0.84 (CV ≈ 0.87), and log-target and separate smoker/non-smoker models gave no gain (0.826 and 0.838). Tuning added about +0.007 CV R² over default boosting. The remaining error (typical miss ≈ ₹2.7k) is driven by information not in the data (diagnoses, hospitalizations), so I would not promise more accuracy from these six fields. A well-engineered linear model matches the tuned trees, so it is a good transparent choice for pricing; use the tuned Gradient Boosting for scoring. Caveat: the split is one 80/20 draw, so the test R² carries roughly ±0.03 uncertainty. XGBoost/LightGBM could not be installed in my environment, so they aren’t compared; they are unlikely to beat 0.84 on 1,338 rows.

Part D – Python

The full Jupyter notebook (Medibuddy_Analysis.ipynb) follows the Workflow.xlsx order: libraries → load → merge → gender/charges histogram → mean charges → Q1–Q8 → models → tuning → diagnostics → saved model. Note that Workflow.xlsx says read_csv/concat, but your files are Excel and need a join on Policy no., so the notebook uses read_excel and merge.
